title: Sovereign wealth funds' China and Hong Kong investments surge 190% after a bruising slump
description: LANZHOU, CHINA - SEPTEMBER 29: Flowers and Chinese national flags decorate the Jinyan Yellow River Bridge on September 29, 2026 in Lanzhou, Gansu Prov
body: LANZHOU, CHINA - SEPTEMBER 29: Flowers and Chinese national flags decorate the Jinyan Yellow River Bridge on September 29, 2026 in Lanzhou, Gansu Province of China. China News Service | Getty ImagesSovereign wealth funds are pouring billions of dollars back into mainland China and Hong Kong, reversing a sharp investment slump, with Middle Eastern investors leading the charge. Investments into mainland China and Hong Kong surged to $14.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026, surging 190% compared with the funds' investments through the entire 2025, according to data provided to CNBC by Singapore-based consultancy Global SWF. That's in stark contrast to a 54% plunge in 2025 from the prior year as geopolitical tensions and concerns over China's economic outlook weighed on investor sentiment.The resurgence this year has been driven largely by Middle Eastern sovereign investors, with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund alone accounting for $6 billion of the inflows, followed by Abu Dhabi Investment Authority's $2.5 billion, data from Global SWF showed. Abu Dhabi's Mubadala and Qatar Investment Authority have invested $800 million and $600 million, respectively.Together, the four Gulf funds accounted for nearly 70% of sovereign investments into China and Hong Kong during the period, underscoring the growing role of Middle Eastern capital in the region.Renewed interest in China comes as sovereign investors increasingly look beyond geopolitical tensions to capitalize on opportunities in Chinese technology, biotechnology, consumer businesses and advanced manufacturing."I think China has gone from 'China is not investable’ to ‘is China investable?’ to today, the most common question I get is: ‘are we missing out?'" said Jenny Lee, senior managing partner at investment management firm Granite Asia.Lee said China's established strengths in manufacturing and biotechnology could give it an advantage as AI development increasingly expands beyond frontier models into industry-specific applications, including robotics and drug discovery.China's extensive network of factories and research laboratories provides access to real-world data that could become increasingly valuable in developing these applications, she added.Drawing interestFor Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala, Asia in general has become an increasingly important destination as the sovereign investor seeks to diversify its portfolio and deepen exposure to long-term growth opportunities.Andrew Wang, who leads consumer division for private equity at Mubadala, said the firm sees compelling opportunities in China, citing attractive valuations and the country's vast consumer market as the fund continues to expand its presence in Asia."Valuations are lower than they've been in years. I think this will be a really good vintage for investors in China," Wang told CNBC. He said China was the fund's top priority for consumer investments in Asia, pointing to the potential for household consumption to expand and the growing competitiveness of Chinese brands.Chinese companies were increasingly moving beyond their reputation for producing inexpensive goods toward higher-value products, Wang said, as homegrown brands demonstrate stronger innovation and competitiveness globally. Mubadala announced a minority investment in China's Luckin Coffee in September, as part of a roughly $1 billion deal alongside Centurium Capital.From caution to conviction?Other big funds have also shown interest this year.Qatar Investment Authority and Norway's sovereign wealth fund participated in Alibaba's $10.2 billion share offering in August, while Singapore's Temasek is identifying opportunities in China, particularly in biotechnology, domestic consumer brands and AI-related hardware."China continues to be interesting," said Rohit Sipahimalani, Temasek's chief investment officer, at the Milken Summit in Singapore recently."Biotech in particular [is] a very exciting area out there which we're investing in. Local consumer brands could really be important," he said.Sipahimalani also pointed to China's growing competitiveness across the AI hardware supply chain, predicting that Chinese manufacturers could increasingly challenge established global players.Temasek was among the cornerstone investors in optical-components manufacturer Zhongji Innolight's multibillion-dollar initial public offering in July.Pandu Sjahrir, chief investment officer at Indonesian sovereign wealth fund Danantara, told CNBC that the fund was also looking to expand its cooperation with China beyond its existing partnerships in nickel processing and battery manufacturing, with growing interest in artificial intelligence, robotics, healthcare and energy efficiency. The Indonesian sovereign investor sees opportunities to build on its energy resources to develop AI-related digital infrastructure and downstream industries. “We now already have someone to head North Asia for us. She's also based in China, and her job as a team is "how do we develop long-term partnership, especially in the downstream side?" he said.Despite the sharp rebound, China remains a relatively small destination for sovereign wealth fund capital compared with Western markets.The U.S. attracted $132.4 billion in sovereign investments in the first nine months of 2026, compared with $44.6 billion for Europe and the U.K., according to Global SWF data. China and Hong Kong's $14.2 billion represented just a fraction of those flows.

schema.headline: Sovereign wealth funds' China and Hong Kong investments surge 190% after a bruising slump

title: Southeast Asia is hungry for AI — and the money isn't just in subscriptions
description: SINGAPORE - MAY 31: Scenes of daily life and the urban landscape are seen in Singapore on May 31, 2026. Located at the southern tip of the Malay Penin
body: SINGAPORE - MAY 31: Scenes of daily life and the urban landscape are seen in Singapore on May 31, 2026. Located at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, about 137 kilometers north of the Equator, Singapore is a city-state known for its modern urban environment and high standards of living. Green spaces integrated into the cityscape, multicultural communities and vibrant urban life are among the prominent features of the city. (Photo by Mustafa Hatipoglu/Anadolu via Getty Images)Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesSoutheast Asia is embracing artificial intelligence at a rapid pace. But the business of making money from AI is about more than getting consumers to pay for it.Generative AI adoption in the region has reached around 243 million people in less than three years, according to the annual e-Conomy SEA report released Wednesday by Google, Temasek and Bain & Company. That is equivalent to 58% of the working population, with adoption occurring four times faster than the uptake of mobile internet. Yet only 1% to 2% of the region's population pays for personal AI subscriptions, highlighting a gap between widespread adoption and direct consumer spending.Florian Hoppe, a partner at Bain & Company, told CNBC in an interview that businesses have found other ways to generate AI's commercial value from online shopping to digital advertising.Companies have been using AI to improve e-commerce conversion rates and handle routine customer inquiries, allowing employees to focus on other tasks, he added. Consumers may also be paying indirectly for AI when purchasing products developed using the technology.The findings come as Southeast Asia's digital economy is projected to grow 17% to $368 billion in gross merchandise value this year, with the market expected to exceed $1 trillion by 2035, according to the report.Hoppe also pointed to another factor driving the region's enthusiasm for AI: its willingness to embrace new technologies as consumers have shown what he described as "pragmatic optimism" toward AI, embracing the technology for its practical benefits. The region has historically ranked among the most active users of major digital platforms on a per-capita basis. "They're very experimental," Hoppe said, describing consumers' openness to new tools and services. He also added that in terms of individual markets, Singapore is among Southeast Asia's early leaders in AI adoption.That openness is extending to more autonomous uses of AI, with 75% of users willing to let AI agents find the best prices and complete purchases on their behalf. The report shows that confidence is also growing, with 62% of respondents saying they trust AI tools more than they did a year ago.Despite the rapid adoption, people in Southeast Asia still use AI far less than those in the U.S., with usage per person at just 10% of U.S. levels.For businesses, however, the potential returns are becoming more tangible. About 69% of shoppers use AI to compare complex purchases such as electronics, while early case studies show AI helping businesses boost conversion rates by 10% year on year and increase the average amount customers spend per order by as much as 75%.An example is Shopee, a Southeast Asian e-commerce platform, which now handles approximately 80% of customer queries through AI chatbots, helping cut its cost per customer contact by 30% year on year.In online media, Hoppe pointed to a "significant uplift" in advertising click-through rates and conversions through AI-powered advertising and improved targeting.But the benefits extend beyond online shopping. AI is helping travelers plan trips, making digital advertising more effective and enabling voice-assisted bookings for ride-hailing and food delivery services.Southeast Asia's online travel market is projected to grow 10% to $59 billion in gross merchandise value this year. Online media revenue, including digital advertising and streaming, is expected to rise 22% to $44 billion, while ride-hailing and food delivery are forecast to grow 15% to $40 billion in gross merchandise value, according to the report.

schema.headline: Southeast Asia is hungry for AI — and the money isn't just in subscriptions

title: United Airlines set to open its biggest airport lounge in $2.6 billion overhaul at Houston hub
description: United is opening its largest-ever airport lounge in George Bush Intercontinental Airport.Courtesy: United AirlinesUnited Airlines is set to open its
body: United is opening its largest-ever airport lounge in George Bush Intercontinental Airport.Courtesy: United AirlinesUnited Airlines is set to open its biggest airport lounge this week, which it says is the largest in the Americas, as airlines continue to plow money into the facilities for high-spending customers.The 54,000-square-foot lounge is opening Thursday at George Bush Intercontinental Airport's Terminal B in Houston, part of an overhaul of the facility that includes 22 gates for mainline aircraft. The airport, with more than 500 departures a day, is United's main connecting hub for flights to and from Latin America.United Airlines' new airport lounge at Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport.Courtesy: United AirlinesThe new club can seat 800 people and features an outdoor terrace for plane-spotting as well as two full-service bars and buffets. The lounge, part of United's $2.6 billion investment at the airport's Terminal B, shows how airlines are putting more money into larger spaces for premium-travel demand to attract the growing ranks of elite frequent flyers, co-branded credit card holders and customers just willing to spend more to fly.United Airlines new airport lounge, the largest in its network, at George Bush Intercontinental Airport.Courtesy: United AirlinesAmerican Airlines earlier this month said it is planning its largest-ever lounge at its Charlotte Douglas International Airport hub in North Carolina. Delta Air Lines has expanded both its popular Delta Sky Clubs and its top-tier Delta One Lounges.Southwest Airlines is building its first-ever network of airport lounges, which are tied to its credit card partner, Chase. Last week, the carrier unveiled mock-ups of the lounges, which it is calling Icon. And JetBlue Airways opened lounges in New York and Boston in the past year.Read more CNBC airline newsWhy airfare could rise even more, but airline profits won’tBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to premium upgradesCompanies spurn airlines’ cheapest business class ticketsUnited’s next decision: What to do with all those Boeing 737 Max 10 seats it ordered years agoRecord heat, crowds drive offseason boom in international travel

schema.headline: United Airlines set to open its biggest airport lounge in $2.6 billion overhaul at Houston hub

title: EBay to lay off 9% of workforce in its second round of job cuts this year
description: Cheng Xin | Getty ImagesEBay will lay off about 9% of its workforce in a move to streamline its operations and focus on its fastest-growing areas, a c
body: Cheng Xin | Getty ImagesEBay will lay off about 9% of its workforce in a move to streamline its operations and focus on its fastest-growing areas, a company spokesperson confirmed to CNBC. The layoffs will affect approximately 1,000 employees. "As we work to capture the significant opportunity ahead, this step was taken to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities," the spokesperson said in a statement.The company also said it will continue to hire in "priority areas aligned with our strategy." As of the end of 2025, eBay had roughly 12,300 employees.Reuters first reported the news, citing a memo to staff from CEO Jamie Iannone that read in part, "Our strategy is working." "Continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest," Iannone said in the memo, seen by Reuters.  This is the second round of layoffs for the online marketplace this year, following a 6% workforce reduction that affected about 800 employees, in February. The company has been steadily shrinking its headcount over recent years at the same time it's ramping up spending on artificial intelligence. EBay also acquired the used clothing resale platform Depop — a brand with a strong customer base of Gen Z and millennial users — from Etsy earlier this year. The $1.4 billion deal was finalized in July. Shares of eBay were up approximately 1% Wednesday morning. — CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed to this report.

schema.headline: EBay to lay off 9% of workforce in its second round of job cuts this year

title: New Mexico AG lawsuit accuses Epstein's attorney and accountant of facilitating sex trafficking
description: Julia Molchanova, left, Anouska De Georgiou, center, and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez speak at a news conference where Torrez announced a l
body: Julia Molchanova, left, Anouska De Georgiou, center, and New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez speak at a news conference where Torrez announced a lawsuit against the co-executors of Jeffrey Epstein's estate, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, in Albuquerque, N.M.Susan Montoya Bryan | APNew Mexico's attorney general on Wednesday filed a federal lawsuit accusing Jeffrey Epstein's long-time personal lawyer and accountant of facilitating Epstein's sex trafficking operation.The civil suit alleges the attorney, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, helped finance and conceal Epstein's sex trafficking, which included the abuse of girls and young women at his Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County, New Mexico.Indyke and Kahn are beneficiaries of Epstein's 1953 Trust, co-executors of Epstein's estate, and administrators of the revocable trust, whose name comes from the year of the convicted sex offender's birth. New Mexico's suit asks a judge to block Indyke and Kahn from receiving payments from the estate as the case proceeds in U.S. District Court in New Mexico. The suit alleges the two men participated in a sex trafficking venture in violation of the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act; and that they violated New Mexico's Racketeering Act by engaging in kidnapping, criminal solicitation and conspiracy.Darren K. Indyke, Jeffrey Epstein's former lawyer, arrives for his deposition before the House Oversight Committee on Capitol Hill, Thursday, March 19, 2026, in Washington.Jose Luis Magana | APAttorney General Raul Torrez's office said Epstein's estate is currently valued at more than $107 million, and the suit says Indyke and Kahn are eligible for bequests of $50 million and $25 million, subject to the availability of funds."Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible," Torrez said in a statement, which was released as he appeared at a press conference flanked by two survivors of abuse by Epstein, Anouska De Georgiou and Julia Molchanova."The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico," Torrez said. "Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences."The suit comes a month after The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York had opened an investigation into Indyke and Kahn.De Georgiou said at the press conference that her abuse by Epstein and his accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell, "did not happen in isolation.""It could not have continued for as long as it did without people facilitating it, looking the other way, or choosing to do nothing to stop it," De Georgiou said. "Accountability cannot end with Epstein and Maxwell. It must extend to those who knowingly made their abuse possible, especially those who stand to profit from it. That includes anyone who knowingly helped make Epstein appear legitimate to conceal his abuse of women and girls."Zorro Ranch, Jeffrey Epstein's New Mexico property.Courtesy: U.S. District Court of New Mexico | State of New Mexico v. Darren Indyke | Richard KahnDaniel Weiner, an attorney for Epstein's estate, in a statement to CNBC, said, "Both Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn reject as categorically false the allegations that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr. Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of Mr. Epstein's actions while they provided legal or accounting services to him.""They are confident that they will prevail on the claims asserted against them," Weiner said."Neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General's investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit," Weiner said. "Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have given multiple depositions in civil lawsuits and have testified at length before the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Government Reform," the attorney said. "Had the New Mexico Attorney General wanted to learn the actual facts of their professional services for Epstein, the Attorney General or his staff could have reached out to schedule interviews.  Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have cooperated with any and all investigations when asked to do so."Richard Kahn, an accountant for convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, arrives for a House Oversight Committee deposition about Epstein on Capitol Hill on Wednesday, March 11, 2026.Tom Williams | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesThe lawsuit alleges Indyke and Kahn personally profited from their relationship to Epstein, who killed himself in a federal jail in New York in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on child sex trafficking charges."Between 2011 and 2019, Indyke received more than $16 million from Epstein and related entities, and Kahn received more than $10 million," Torrez's office said in a statement. Torrez, at a press conference Wednesday, said his office is continuing a criminal investigation of Epstein's sex trafficking operation. No criminal charges have been filed in connection with that probe.Epstein's estate in February agreed to pay out as much as $35 million to settle a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Manhattan that accused Indyke and Kahn of aiding and abetting Epstein's sex trafficking.The proposed settlement does not include any admission of misconduct by Indyke or Kahn. The judge handling the case last month endorsed a proposal by the suit's plaintiff to notify potential class members to submit claims on the settlement by conducting a four-week-long social media campaign on Facebook and Instagram.

schema.headline: New Mexico AG lawsuit accuses Epstein's attorney and accountant of facilitating sex trafficking

title: Bank of Korea holds rates after President Lee calls for boosting housing supply
description: Shin Hyun Song, governor of the Bank of Korea, during a fireside chat at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangk
body: Shin Hyun Song, governor of the Bank of Korea, during a fireside chat at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.  Sirachai Arunrugstichai | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSouth Korea's central bank expectedly kept its policy rate steady at 3% on Thursday, after two straight hikes, with analysts pointing that it does not signal a change in policy stance as inflation stays elevated.Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the Bank of Korea to hold rates, and the decision comes after President Lee Jae Myung reportedly called for an "all out effort" to boost housing supply. The BOK in its statement said it opted to hold rates as it assesses the effects of the two prior rate hikes, and looks at "developments in both domestic and external risk factors," citing increasing uncertainties around the Middle East conflict and monetary and fiscal policies of major economies.Last week, BOK Governor Shin Hyun Song said at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings that the central bank will keep monetary policy restrictive until it's confident that inflation was heading back to target. "Inflation has really picked up, both from the cost-push and the demand-pull," Shin said. Inflation in Asia's fourth-largest economy came in at 2.9% in September, staying at or above the BOK's 2% target for 13 months. As President Lee pushes for increasing the housing supply, the BOK on Thursday flagged that "housing-related loans continued to increase and the pace of increase in housing prices in Seoul and its surrounding areas accelerated again."The Kospi was trading 1.23% lower, while the won strengthened marginally against the dollar to trade at 1,326.1. Given a strong economy and persistent inflation, a pause does not mean the end of the tightening cycle, according to Gareth Leather, senior Asia economist at Capital Economics. Leather foresees one more hike at BOK's meeting next month. South Korea's growth has been largely supported by exports of semiconductors as demand for chips to power the AI boom continues. Exports in September skyrocketed at a record 83.7% year on year, with semiconductor shipments surging 263% compared to the same period last year.The IMF has projected the country's growth at 3.3% for the whole of 2026. GDP growth for the country came in at 3.8% and 3.7% for the first and second quarters respectively, both times beating expectations. — CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Bank of Korea holds rates after President Lee calls for boosting housing supply

title: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds
description: Rick Rieder speaking at the CNBC CEO Council Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 2, 2026.Aaron Clamage | CNBCInvestors may be wary of the volatility hi
body: Rick Rieder speaking at the CNBC CEO Council Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 2, 2026.Aaron Clamage | CNBCInvestors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration."Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday. That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus. The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconiShares Flexible Income Active ETF year to dateBest opportunities include hyperscalersRieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3. That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG. "They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it." Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%. That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised."Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names. "There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits. CoreWeave's 2031 bond yield on Oct. 21, 2026Fed watchRieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool. The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said."They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added. Calculating risks aheadRieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026."The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched. "With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

schema.headline: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

title: James Talarico fires back at Elon Musk in Texas Senate race feud
description: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico speaks at the Hilton University of Houston on Oct. 21, 2026 in Houston, Texas.Danielle Villasana | Ge
body: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico speaks at the Hilton University of Houston on Oct. 21, 2026 in Houston, Texas.Danielle Villasana | Getty ImagesJames Talarico, the Democratic nominee seeking a Senate seat from Texas, fired back Wednesday night at Elon Musk for an X post in which the world's richest man hours earlier had said, "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico.""There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal U.S. Senator," Talarico wrote in reply to Musk's tweet.Talarico earlier Wednesday, during a campaign speech at the UH Hilton on the main campus of the University of Houston, called out Musk."In all likelihood, if you've seen an attack ad on your screen, that was Elon. If you've gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon," Talarico said, according to a report by Houston Public Media."If you've received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon too," Talarico said. "Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our taxpayer dollars. He wants his very own personal United States Senator. He is trying to buy Texas. But on Nov. 3, we are going to send a clear message to the world's first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale."SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a press briefing held by President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026.Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesThe sniping between Musk and Talarico came five days after news broke that Musk donated $158 million to a Republican super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, in September. That money ended up with Texas PAC, a group that is backing Talarico's opponent, GOP nominee Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general.Musk also sent $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, another group that is backing Paxton.Musk, who is CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, executed the big money dump as polls showed Paxton trailing Talarico in the contest.Talarico's campaign last week said he had raised $64 million in the third quarter of this year. That was the largest tally ever reported for a Senate candidate in a third quarter, his campaign said. In comparison, Paxton's campaign raised just $18 million for the same quarter.Paxton beat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary earlier this year. His campaign didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

schema.headline: James Talarico fires back at Elon Musk in Texas Senate race feud

title: Critical web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond
description: 21 October 2026, Baden-Württemberg, Stuttgart: When visiting the website of the Baden-Württemberg Ministry of the Interior, a warning message appears
body: 21 October 2026, Baden-Württemberg, Stuttgart: When visiting the website of the Baden-Württemberg Ministry of the Interior, a warning message appears in the browser indicating a potential security issue. A serious security vulnerability is threatening websites worldwide; blogs, online stores, and news portals could become targets for attackers. The PHP vulnerability allows attackers to take over entire servers. Photo: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa (Photo by Bernd Weißbrod/picture alliance via Getty Images)Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesThe tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet.The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems.The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks.The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesday urged organizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible.The Federal Bureau of Investigation also warned that malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk.Cybersecurity authorities in Singapore, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and the European Union have issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems. Amazon said its threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure.Meanwhile, Google and OpenAI highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in identifying and addressing cybersecurity threats. Google said its cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches.OpenAI said researchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The company said it had spent the past two months leading a coalition of software maintainers, cybersecurity researchers and security providers to coordinate fixes and prepare protective measures ahead of public disclosure.The ChatGPT maker described the flaws as among the most significant security issues in recent memory, highlighting both the potential of advanced AI systems to identify vulnerabilities in widely used software and the risk that similar capabilities could be exploited by cybercriminals.Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services, said it had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates.The PHP development team has released security fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. The episode underscores how vulnerabilities in widely used software can pose risks across industries and borders, even as AI increasingly plays a role in helping security researchers uncover and address those weaknesses.

schema.headline: Critical web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond

title: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
description: Workers install roofing for a new home under construction in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, June 29, 2026.Zak Bennett | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Fede
body: Workers install roofing for a new home under construction in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, June 29, 2026.Zak Bennett | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist.Housing data deteriorated further in September, according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates.Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage."The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze."The National Association of Realtors reported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%.Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday. watch nowPrivately owned housing starts fell 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data.Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023."Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates."Rising rates weigh on outlookThe rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices.Outside of the pending sales number, home builder sentiment is at lows not seen in 14 years.Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs.  But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control. Readings last week on consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009.Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing.However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday."In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months."More of the sameSeveral data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. Goldman forecasts residential investment to decline 2.5%, 4% and 1%, respectively, over the coming three quarters, with a possibility for a steeper decline if mortgage rates don't fall.The firm sees single-family starts of just 875,000 in 2027, little changed from this year, while existing sales are forecast at 3.9 million, also about the same as 2026 but notably 26% below pre-Covid 2019 levels. Walker attributed the middling levels as a product of the "lock-in" effect in which it's too expensive for current homeowners to move and take on higher borrowing costs while deteriorating affordability weighs on new construction."Housing activity has remained rangebound in recent years, capped on the upside by affordability headwinds and buffered on the downside by the longstanding housing shortage," Walker wrote. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity."Markets expect the Fed to hold benchmark rates steady when it meets next week. However, futures pricing implies a strong chance of a quarter-point hike in December and another in March 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.One point of optimism comes from Yun, the NAR economist, who thinks the trend of mortgage costs running ahead of Fed hikes could mean that rates are topping out."Given that mortgage rates have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve's short-term interest rate hikes, mortgage rates could be topping out," he said. "Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably."watch now

schema.headline: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes

title: Trump denies ordering Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, says he doesn't know who did
description: watch nowPresident Donald Trump on Wednesday insisted he had nothing to do with a slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink in Ukraine and said he does not know i
body: watch nowPresident Donald Trump on Wednesday insisted he had nothing to do with a slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink in Ukraine and said he does not know if Elon Musk was responsible for speed-capping the critical satellite service.Trump's latest denial came one day after The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, reported Musk ordered the slowdown and discussed it with Trump."I wasn't involved," Trump told a reporter when asked about the decision as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in South Carolina.When pressed to answer if Musk, SpaceX's founder and CEO, ordered the slowdown, Trump said, "I don't know who did it, but I was not involved."The recent disruption of Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, rendered some Ukrainian drones effectively useless, weakening defenses against Russian attacks.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said his military still faces "speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield services in different parts of the front.""No explanation for either of these issues has been provided to Ukraine by the American side," he said.The Journal reported Tuesday that Musk and Trump discussed the move to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, citing two people familiar with the matter.One of the people who spoke with the news outlet claimed Musk discussed the matter with multiple senior administration officials, including Trump himself, prior to imposing the Starlink speed cap.Trump and Musk have both recently ramped up their criticism of Zelenskyy. But neither of them has yet identified who ordered the Starlink disruption.Musk said on X last week that Starshield systems are "owned and controlled by the US government" and that any speed or usage limits are "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Earlier Wednesday, Zelesnkyy said he and Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik "discussed in detail launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors.""We will involve partners who have the capacity to provide support," Zelenskyy said in an X post.Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday morning that he does not believe Musk would throttle Starlink without "at least the acquiescence of the White House."watch now

title: Southwest Airlines cuts 2026 profit forecast on higher fuel
description: A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 airplane departs from San Diego International Airport on May 27, 2026.Kevin Carter | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesS
body: A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 airplane departs from San Diego International Airport on May 27, 2026.Kevin Carter | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesSouthwest Airlines became the third major U.S. airline this month to cut its 2026 profit forecast due to higher fuel prices, but CEO Bob Jordan said travelers continue to book despite higher fares.The carrier expects to earn between $2.60 and $2.85 a share on an adjusted basis this year, down from its forecast in July of between $3.25 to as much as $4.25 a share.Here's what Southwest reported for third quarter compared with Wall Street expectations, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:Earnings per share: 66 cents adjusted vs. 58 cents expectedRevenue: $8.42 billion adjusted vs. $8.25 billion expectedSouthwest forecast per-share adjusted earnings of between 55 cents and 80 cents in the fourth quarter and unit revenue, a gauge of airfare, up as much as 21% from a year earlier. It said it expects to grow capacity by up to 4% year over year."Demand remained strong as we lapped last year's bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we've built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs," Jordan said in an earnings release.The airline said its average passenger fare was $231.69 in the third quarter, up almost 27% from the same quarter of 2025. A spokesman said that number does not include add-on fees. The number of revenue passengers carried fell 3.2% to 33.47 million people.Under pressure to grow revenue, Southwest has been remaking its longtime business model over the past several years, scrapping its old policies like two free checked bags per passenger and open seating. In its place, Southwest has started charging for many seat assignments and added a bag fee, similar to major competitors.For the third quarter, Southwest posted net income of $270 million, or 55 cents a share, up from $54 million or 10 cents a share a year earlier. Revenue rose more than 21% to $8.42 billion.Adjusting for one-time items, Southwest reported 66 cents a share.Delta Air Lines and United Airlines also cut their profit outlooks for the rest of the year when they reported third-quarter earnings. Both of those airlines reported top- and bottom-line misses for the third quarter.Read more CNBC airline newsWhy airfare could rise even more, but airline profits won’tBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to premium upgradesCompanies spurn airlines’ cheapest business class ticketsUnited’s next decision: What to do with all those Boeing 737 Max 10 seats it ordered years agoRecord heat, crowds drive offseason boom in international travel

title: Mortgage rates drop for the first time in 2 months, but demand still falls further
description: Homes in Daly City, California, US, on Tuesday, May 19, 2026. Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMortgage demand took another leg lower, despite a
body: Homes in Daly City, California, US, on Tuesday, May 19, 2026. Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMortgage demand took another leg lower, despite a brief respite from rising interest rates.Total mortgage application volume fell 5.3% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, dropped last week to 7.41% from 7.50%, with points falling to 0.75 from 0.83 including the origination fee for loans with a 20% down payment. "Mortgage rates decreased for the first time in over two months," said Joel Kan, an MBA economist, in a release. "However, lower rates were not enough to boost application activity, as both purchase and refinance applications continued to decline." Applications to refinance a home loan, which are most sensitive to weekly moves, fell just 2% week to week, a smaller drop than some previous weeks when rates were moving higher. Refinance demand was still 59% lower than the same week one year ago. With rates now over a full percentage point higher than they were a year ago, there is a very small pool of borrowers who can benefit from a refinance.Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home declined a steeper 7% for the week and were 18% lower from the year before. Buyers are reacting less to the weekly move in rates but more to the overall higher level. A report from the National Association of Realtors on Tuesday showed a sharp drop in September pending home sales. These are measured by signed contracts, so it showed the real-time impact of rising rates during the month. Rates remained at that higher level in October. Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.For those buyers in the market, a continued high share are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs, which offer lower rates but are considered riskier because they will eventually reset to whatever the market rate is at the end of their term. "The ARM share held steady at 10.5 percent, as ARM rates remained almost a full percentage point lower than the 30-year fixed rate, giving qualified borrowers a lower rate option to purchase a home," Kan added. Mortgage rates haven't done much to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. Last week was a particularly volatile week for rates, due to multiple monthly inflation reports. This week the moves have seemed to follow oil prices."But we'd caution against placing too much emphasis on the oil price correlation," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. "It's been highly unreliable for more than a month." Correction: The National Association of Realtors on Tuesday reported September pending home sales. An earlier version misstated the day.

title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.
body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026. Brendan McDermid | ReutersMeta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion."The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full."For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal.""This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."Read more CNBC tech newsMeta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reactionTesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declinesIntel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind scheduleInvestors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are risingMeta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg-led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users, raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.  Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.  Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.WATCH: AI oversight is the topic of discourse in Washington.watch now

schema.headline: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case

title: Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that’s at least 5 years behind schedule
description: Intel announced on Oct. 21, 2026, that crews have installed the first major structural truss at its new chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio.Cou
body: Intel announced on Oct. 21, 2026, that crews have installed the first major structural truss at its new chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio.Courtesy: IntelIntel has hit a milestone in the construction of its massive chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio, that's running at least five years behind schedule, a delay that's coincided with soaring demand for advanced chips. On Wednesday, Intel announced that crews have installed the first major structural truss in Ohio, which means the next part of the construction has finally begun. "This represents another significant step toward expanded U.S. leading-edge semiconductor capacity," Intel Foundry head Naga Chandrasekaran wrote in a post on the company's website on Wednesday. Intel still needs customers to make the investment pay off.In September, reports surfaced that the world's leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, SK Hynix, could team up with Intel in Ohio to lease some foundry space to make memory chips at the new site. Neither company would confirm any plans.When Intel first announced the Ohio factory in 2022, it was expected to start delivering chips in 2025. Intel pushed back that timeline, now aiming to finish construction in 2030. A second Ohio fab is also planned for completion in 2031 at the site, just northeast of Columbus.The delay reflects a broader recalibration of Intel's foundry ambitions under CEO Lip-Bu Tan.The Ohio factory is only one piece of Intel's ambitious build-out to start making chips for outside customers that began under former CEO Pat Gelsinger. When Tan took the helm in 2025, his turnaround strategy was more cautious, choosing to wait for customer demand before forging ahead with ambitious chip fab plans.Still, by late 2025, Intel was in high-volume production at its Arizona chip fab, producing its most advanced 18A chips. On Wednesday, Chandrasekaran also announced that operations at its next fab in Arizona are expected to begin by the end of 2028.But Intel has yet to land a major external customer for those 18A chips coming out of Arizona. Instead, Intel is using them to make its own processors for devices.Once a dominant force in the chip manufacturing landscape, Intel hit major delays with its 7- and 10-nanometer nodes, triggering the stock's worst year ever in 2024. Customers have been reluctant to commit again since.Now, Intel's window of opportunity may have arrived alongside record demand for AI, as leading chip manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. can't make chips fast enough. Even for the biggest chipmakers like  Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Apple and Broadcom,  "competition is extremely fierce," to get space on TSMC's factory lines, according to Mizuho Securities analyst Jordan Klein.Intel could offer customers an alternative source for chip production, according to TechInsights analyst Dan Hutcheson."People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Hutcheson said. "All the big ones have been testing there."WATCH: Inside Intel’s new Arizona fab, where the chipmaker’s fate hangs in the balancewatch now

schema.headline: Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that’s at least 5 years behind schedule
